heroLead: New Kensington grew up as an aluminum town along the Allegheny River, and like a lot of Westmoreland County's older industrial communities, its mineral history is tangled up with the surface development that came before shale gas.
intro: The city itself is mostly built over, but the mineral estate underneath doesn't disappear just because industry and housing covered the ground. If your family retained oil and gas rights from land that later became part of New Kensington's growth, or from farmland in the surrounding townships, those rights are still worth evaluating on their own.
We buy mineral and royalty interests connected to New Kensington directly. We trace the title ourselves through the county recorder and explain what we find in plain terms.

sections.heading: An Industrial City's Buried Mineral Estate
paragraphs: Aluminum manufacturing shaped New Kensington's development in the twentieth century, and industrial-era land transactions sometimes handled mineral rights differently than a straightforward farm sale would have. Confirming what survived those transactions, separate from the surface, is part of the title work we do.

The surrounding Westmoreland County townships have seen Marcellus and deeper Utica leasing activity over the past decade and a half, and interests tied to that acreage are what we're most often evaluating in this area.

sections.heading: Researching an Industrial-Era Deed
paragraphs: We pull your chain of title through the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds in Greensburg, working through older industrial-era conveyances where necessary to confirm exactly what your family holds today.
This kind of research can take longer than a simple rural farm title, but it's the only way to give you a confident answer.

sections.heading: What We'll Explain Before Any Offer
paragraphs: Once title is confirmed, we'll walk through your division order and any royalty history so you understand your interest fully before a number comes up.

faqs.question: Does New Kensington's industrial past affect mineral rights outside the city itself?
faqs.answer: Generally no, industrial-era transactions in the city are usually distinct from farmland mineral history in the surrounding townships, though we verify each parcel individually.

faqs.question: My interest traces back to an old aluminum-era land sale. Can you still confirm it?
faqs.answer: Yes, we're experienced working through older industrial-era deed language to confirm what mineral rights, if any, were carved out or retained.

faqs.question: Is there active drilling connected to New Kensington-area interests?
faqs.answer: We check current activity specific to your parcel's unit as part of our review, since it varies across Westmoreland County.
